...So same explanation as why metronomes sync up on a slightly wobbly table?

There's a subtle difference. This theory allows for vibration within a surface that both clocks commonly share to cause them to fall into sync, where a suspended table (as in the metronome experiment) is due to oscillation of the table -- actual movement -- rather than simple vibration.

Technically both are forms of movement, but the metronome effect is much more pronounced due to actual movement. If placed on an extremely stable surface, you would expect the metronomes to stop moving due to loss of momentum long before they approached comparable synchronization, while the clocks would continue to run and eventually show the effect.

did you play it when it came out?

It moved the genre forward in ways that have almost not been surpassed. First and foremost, it had squad AI. Now a lot of this I later learned was scripted. But in theory, the solders you fought were acting in a coordinated manner. They'd flush you out with grenades and ambush you.

They also did an incredible amount of world building for an FPS. All the alien enemies had a sort of ecosystem they were part of, with predators and pray. The Black Mesa research facility itself had all sorts of weird stories told through the ruined experiments you walk through the aftermath of. Plus this was one of the first games that tried to do the "show don't tell" story approach. Sometimes they'd lock you in a room with an NPC and force you to listen to them talk. But most times events would just trigger as you entered a room.

The weapons actually displayed a lot of creativity as well. Id Software really set a pattern of pistol, shotgun, double barreled shotgun, machine gun, rocket launcher. And sadly, most FPS really stuck to that formula. It's easy to forget what an insane glut of FPSes there were after Doom and Quake, and most of them were just perfunctory serious of levels with ambiguous creativity. Half-Life had a laser that shot through walls, a missile launcher with a laser sight, det packs, laser mines, little critters that ran after people and exploded, and a fucking Ghost Busters energy ray.

Then there were some interesting technical things too. Like having mouths that actually attempted to mimic the audio that was being played. And NPCs you needed to lead around so they could open doors for you. It also had a few really interesting bosses that weren't just bullet sponges, but instead required you to solve environmental puzzles to beat them.

In some ways, I still don't think Half-Life has been surpassed, not even by Half-Life 2.

Both games had revolutionary levels of interactivity with the environment and reactivity of the AI, for their respective times.

A great deal of that was lots of smoke and mirrors, but they were good smoke and mirrors and did a very good job at convincing the player that the game / AI seems to be a lot more complex than it really is. Valve spends very, very much work on small details and polishing, and getting small and simple pieces (like simple AI scripting routines with fixed waypoints) to work together to convey the illusion of a much more complex and impressive system (like a seemingly life-like, complex and very reactive AI behavior).

A bit more specifically, HL1 was essentially the first FPS with interactive, real-time "cutscenes", where shit would explode and half of the level would collapse, helicopters would fly in and mow crap down but you could shoot them down at any point, and all of those environmental effects would seemingly dynamically affect enemies as well. HL2 continued that with the integration of physics and it was kind of the first game to allow the player to utilize physics in such a sandbox-like way.

That aside, the games were generally graphically impressive if not 100%, pushing-the-limits state of the art and generally much, much more polished and bug-free than comparable games of their respective eras, the gameplay was solid and the entire experience was just high quality.

The games might not seem that out of the ordinary by today's standards, but it's important to judge them in the context of their times.

I honestly wish that HL3 comes with a lot better AI that isn't just heavily scripted, but is actually good no matter where you drop them in a game world. That way you can more easily make maps for it.

That said. I hope to god they finally make Hammer easier to use.
